inv.name: The invention
inv.title: The Revolutionary Invention
inv.text:
For days, (Inventor) has been experimenting with a peculiar idea. Now (inventor.he/she) has summoned the villagers to witness the result. A woven mat covers the work, and a nervous apprentice stands nearby holding a gourd of water in case something goes wrong.
"This," announces (Inventor), "may change everything."
An elder asks whether it will at least be useful. (Inventor) hesitates. "That remains to be seen."

disc.name: The discovery
disc.title: The Revolutionary Discovery
disc.text:
While working near the {beach|forest|garden|waterfall|fire pit|research area|night sky}, (Inventor) notices something nobody in the village has ever described before. After repeated observations, (inventor.he/she) concludes that it may change the way Isola understands the world.
The researchers demand proof. The elders demand an explanation. A child asks whether the discovery is edible.

b1.text: THE MASTER SCHOLAR: The idea withstands scrutiny; (Inventor) is invited to become one of the island's leading scholars.

b2.text: THE UNEXPECTED FLAW: An apprentice spots a serious problem. The invention is revised, or the discovery is reinterpreted.

b3.text: THE SCHOLARLY FEUD: Two researchers claim credit for the breakthrough. The elders must settle the dispute.

b4.text: THE IMPOSSIBLE RESULT: Repeated tests confirm something that seems to defy ordinary explanation. A rare mystery begins.

b5.text: THE FALSE DISCOVERY: A careful experiment disproves the claim. (Inventor) is disappointed but gains knowledge from the attempt.

b6.text: THE ACCIDENTAL ADVANCE: The original idea is useless, but the failed experiment reveals something genuinely valuable.

c1.text: THE PERFECTED DESIGN: A flaw is corrected; the invention becomes reliable or the discovery becomes reproducible.

c2.text: THE SHATTERING: A brittle model cracks into countless pieces. The inventor survives, embarrassed and covered in fragments.

c3.text: THE EXPLOSION: A rare fictional experimental mishap produces a startling bang and destroys the demonstration apparatus. Nearby villagers retreat; damaged equipment must be replaced.

c4.text: THE DISAPPEARANCE: The object or phenomenon vanishes before the scholars can document it. Nobody believes the witnesses.

text_only.reason: narrative: the object or the idea vanishes, not a villager

c5.text: THE DISINTEGRATION: An exceptionally rare impossible device crumbles into dust, leaving no usable remains.

c6.text: THE SECOND MIRACLE: Repetition works even better than the first attempt. The village celebrates a genuine breakthrough.

c7.text: THE SMALL IMPROVEMENT: The second version is less spectacular but more useful. (Inventor) learns the value of patient work.

d1.text: THE HIDDEN GENIUS: The invention quietly improves the lives of a few villagers before the rest learn of it.

d2.text: THE STOLEN CREDIT: A rival unveils the same idea first. A witness or notebook may eventually establish the truth.

d5.text: THE RELUCTANT CELEBRITY: The secret leaks and (Inventor) becomes famous despite desperately wishing to be left alone.

d6.text: THE DANGEROUS RUMOR: Villagers mistake secrecy for evidence of sorcery or dealings with outsiders. An elder investigates.

e1.text: OFFICIAL ADOPTION: The elders approve practical use, training, or preservation of the discovery in the village records.

e2.text: THE PROHIBITION: The elders ban it, fearing waste, conflict, or harm. Some villagers continue debating the decision.

e3.text: THE LONG DEBATE: The council argues until sunset and reaches no conclusion. (Inventor) falls asleep during the final speech.

e4.text: THE PUBLIC TEST: A fair demonstration settles the question, though the outcome may be triumph, embarrassment, or mystery.

e5.text: THE COMPROMISE: Limited use is permitted while researchers continue investigating; reputations remain divided.

items.text: TWO LAYERS OF BREAD WITH A COOKED MEAT FILLING - A flat round of seasoned meat between two soft pieces of bread, with leaves or relish if available. The villagers debate whether it is a meal or merely an improperly assembled loaf.
THINLY CUT GARDEN LEAVES AND VEGETABLES IN A TANGY DRESSING - The cook claims raw plants can be an entire dish. Some are delighted; others demand to know when the actual food will arrive.
FLAT ROUND CAKES - A cook presses dough into circles and cooks it on a heated stone. It may be soft, crisp, thick, thin, sweet, or folded around other food.
CRUNCHY FOLDED SHELLS - Thin cooked cakes are bent while warm and filled with meat, beans, fish, or vegetables. The first taster cracks the shell and showers the ground with dinner.
THE BUBBLING DRINK - A sealed or naturally effervescent drink releases startling bubbles. A child declares that the drink is trying to escape.
THE DELICATE FISH PLATE - Exceptionally fresh fish is cut into elegant thin pieces and arranged with painstaking care. A hungry villager asks why the cook has forgotten the fire.
SWEETENED SNOW OR ICE - Rare ice or snow obtained by a fantastic accident, a high mountain, or magical intervention is mixed with fruit or sweetness. It melts before half the judges can taste it.
A NEW BREADFRUIT PREPARATION - The fruit is roasted, pounded, steamed, or shaped in an unprecedented way. Some call it genius; others say it is still just breadfruit.
A COLOR-CHANGING LIQUID - A flower extract shifts color when mixed with different substances. Scholars investigate what the change signifies; a prankster wants to color everyone's soup.
AN UNUSUAL CRYSTAL - A transparent mineral bends light in an unexpected way, leading to optical experiments and wild rumors.
A NEW RULE OF NATURE - (Inventor) identifies a repeatable pattern in water, falling fruit, shadows, plants, or tides. It is a discovery even if nothing physical has been manufactured.
A FLOATING BALL OF LIGHT - A rare, explicitly impossible or magical phenomenon appears over a bowl of water or carved stone. Scholars cannot decide whether to study it or run away.
A GAS THAT MAKES A STRANGE SOUND - A sealed vessel produces a peculiar hiss when opened. The inventor is more impressed than the villagers, who insist the vessel is simply rude.
A NEW HEALING PREPARATION - A healer proposes an unfamiliar remedy. Responsible tests may show promise, no benefit, or harmful effects.
THE STAR-TRACKING GEARS - Interlocking carved wheels and markers model the movement of stars or planets. The mechanism may help with calendars or navigation, or jam during its unveiling.
THE COUNTING WHEELS - A system of pebbles, notches, cords, or rotating disks helps perform arithmetic. A master scholar praises it; a child computes the answer faster in (child.his/her) head.
THE WATER-LIFTING MACHINE - A wooden and woven-fiber mechanism raises water from a lower pool to a garden. It may work beautifully or soak its inventor and everyone watching.
THE UNLIKELY BRIDGE - An unusual arrangement of timber, vines, and stone supports surprising weight, until an overlooked knot becomes the most important detail in the village.
THE MEMORY STONE - A strangely responsive slab seems to hold symbols, sounds, or recollections. Some fear it contains a spirit; others call it the greatest archive imaginable.
THE NEW GEOMETRY - A researcher proves a surprising relationship among shapes using shells, cords, and marks in the sand.
THE BETTER CALENDAR - A villager finds a more reliable way to anticipate seasons, tides, or astronomical events.

THE SHELL ACCOUNTING SYSTEM - A new method records exchanges, debts, food shares, and communal supplies with shells or knots. Merchants rejoice; others complain that every coconut now has paperwork, though no paper is involved.
THE FAIR EXCHANGE RULE - A villager proposes a new principle for barter. It may reduce arguments or start the longest argument yet.
THE SHARED WORK PLAN - A new arrangement of tasks makes building and harvesting more efficient, unless nobody agrees who starts.
THE IMPOSSIBLE PROOF - A philosopher offers a startling argument that overturns a familiar assumption. The village debates it for days; the fisherman keeps fishing.
THE NEW DANCE - (Inventor) invents a peculiar sequence of steps, turns, and claps. Within days, everyone may be doing it, including elders who insist they disapprove.
THE NEW CLOTHING STYLE - A fresh way to weave, dye, tie, or drape island fabrics catches attention. Some adore it; others say it looks like someone got tangled in a fishing net.
THE NEW HAIRSTYLE - A striking braid, ornament, or arrangement becomes a fashion sensation - or a brief embarrassment.
THE NEW MUSIC - A rhythmic pattern, song form, or unfamiliar instrument captures the village's imagination.
THE NEW GAME - (Inventor) invents a contest using shells, stones, sticks, or woven balls. The rules become more controversial than the game itself.
THE NEW GREETING - A greeting gesture or phrase spreads rapidly, then causes confusion when visitors do not recognize it.
THE FAD OF THE WEEK - An absurd but harmless habit takes over the village: matching shell necklaces, balancing coconuts, dramatic bows, or elaborate names for ordinary chores.
EVERYONE ADOPTS IT: The innovation becomes part of village life.
EVERYONE SHUNS IT: The idea becomes a cautionary tale.
THE INVENTOR IS CALLED MAD: The villagers dismiss (Inventor), possibly until a later event proves (inventor.him/her) right.
COMPLETE INDIFFERENCE: Villagers resume their daily chores.
HERO'S WELCOME: A celebration honors (Inventor).
CHIEF SCHOLAR: (Inventor) gains a high scholarly reputation.
IMITATION CRAZE: Copycat inventions appear everywhere.
ACCUSATION OF TRICKERY: A hearing clears or censures (Inventor).
RIVALRY: A second inventor attempts to outdo the first.
GENERATIONAL LEGACY: A later villager studies the surviving plans, memories, or records and builds on the idea.
